title: Dispatch-Eligibility Registry for Backup Generators
one_liner: Become the neutral system of record for whether each backup generator may legally run for the grid right now, starting as a Texas SB 6 compliance product and growing into the rail that ERCOT, PJM, utilities and aggregators check before dispatch.
customer: First buyer: environmental and compliance leads at 75 MW+ data centers in Texas, who face the SB 6 disclosure and deploy-on-direction duty and must not violate emissions limits. Then PJM colos that must prove permit compliance to state air agencies and counties. Then DR aggregators, utilities and RTOs that consume the dispatch-eligibility certificate through an API. Later expansion is to hospitals, water utilities and telecom, where the wider standby generator fleet is far larger (widely cited estimates run into the hundreds of GW, which I have not verified).
problem: Backup generation is the largest idle block of capacity, but it can only be called if three things are true at the moment of the call: the engine is permitted for that use, it has hours left in the rolling year, and the trigger is a legally recognized emergency. Today the answer sits in permit PDFs, OEM dashboards and spreadsheets. Regulators cannot see it, so they say no. Aggregators carry enforcement risk and cannot prove compliance. Communities suspect the worst about diesel, which sinks permits. Nobody can be sure that dispatching an engine on a given day will not breach a cap.
solution: A run-hour ledger and certificate service. Step one is software only: an ingest of permit conditions (LLM-structured, attorney-reviewed) plus monthly or continuous hour-meter data from BMS exports, OEM telemetry or a read-only J1939/Modbus tap, with non-resettable meter attestation as a fallback. It computes remaining permitted hours per engine, tags every run with its legal basis (test, maintenance, emergency, directed deployment), auto-generates regulator deviation and compliance reports, and publishes a public disclosure page. Step two is a machine-readable Dispatch Eligibility Certificate (open schema, mapped to OpenADR 3.0 and IEEE 2030.5 event payloads, which carry price and event signals but not legal eligibility). RTOs, utilities and aggregators query it before calling an engine. Step three, once regulators accept the format, is clearing and settlement of permit-cleared MW across the registry.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (2025) makes disclosure and directed deployment of backup generation a legal duty for 75 MW+ loads, with an explicit emissions carve-out, so demand for exactly this record is forced by regulation. PJM is filing a reliability backstop and connect-and-manage framework, and Pennsylvania is pushing bring-your-own-generation rules. Turbines are sold out to about 2029-30. LLM extraction of permit conditions cuts the cost of structuring each site from consultant weeks to hours plus attorney QA. None of this existed at scale in 2019.
revenue_model: Onboarding and permit structuring of $15-40k per facility. SaaS of $3-6k per engine per year, which is about $25-50k a year for a 20 MW fleet of 8-10 engines. Aggregators and utilities pay a verification fee of roughly 0.5-1% of dispatch revenue that runs through certificates, and lenders, insurers and RTOs license the data ($100-300k a year). Illustrative scale: 5,000 engines is about $20M ARR, and the roughly 22,000 data center engines implied by 55 GW at 2.5 MW each is about $90M. Wider standby fleets would multiply that several times.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce commodity is not megawatts or even permits. It is remaining permitted run-hours, a finite annual budget per engine, and nobody keeps that ledger neutrally. Whoever holds the ledger regulators trust becomes the rail everyone else must query, and the aggregators cannot build it because they profit from dispatch and cannot credibly police themselves. This inverts the parent: instead of pushing MW into the grid and hoping regulators follow, make regulators' comfort the product. Regulators have said no partly because they cannot see run hours. The registry supplies that visibility and could become the reason a permit is granted with conditions. It also creates network economies (every consumer of the certificate raises the value of being in it) and switching costs, since compliance history is an audit record.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: ship a software-only SB 6 and Title V ledger MVP (permit parsing plus hour-meter ingest plus report generation) and publish the Dispatch Eligibility Certificate v0.1 schema openly. Days 5-30: contact compliance leads at 20 Texas 75 MW+ operators and offer five pilots at $15k with a fixed-format SB 6 backup-generation disclosure pack. Days 10-30: hold informal briefings with TCEQ and VA DEQ staff to test whether an electronic ledger is acceptable as a compliance record, and get consumption LOIs (free API in exchange for feedback) from at least one aggregator. The riskiest assumption is regulator acceptance, so test it in the first month. Retain an air attorney to review the legal-basis tagging.
lineage: mutation of I0836 ('Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Voltus, CPower, Enchanted Rock (ERock), Trinity Consultants (data center and power team). White space: Verification caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted, so no search-engine, Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or TechCrunch queries could be run. I did about 30 direct page fetches and 2 GitHub searches instead. The GitHub searches found no open-source tool for this. I found no company selling a fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' package for existing data center diesel fleets (permit modification, emissions retrofit financing, telemetry, PJM enrollment and M&V). That is absence of evidence from a constrained search, not proof that none exists.

What appears unserved:
(1) A productized, per-state permit playbook tied to capacity outcomes. Trinity-type consultants sell hourly, per-project permitting. DR aggregators (Voltus, CPower) sell enrollment and revenue share. Generator OEMs and ERock sell hardware. Nobody I found owns the seam between them.
(2) Retrofit financing on the subset of engines that need it.
(3) A permit-headroom dataset across Title V and minor-source files.

The binding constraint is legal, not competitive. Under 40 CFR 63.6640(f), as summarized from Cornell LII, emergency engines are limited to 100 hours a year for maintenance, testing and emergencies, with at most 50 of those for non-emergency use. The 50 hours cannot be used for peak shaving or non-emergency demand response, and cannot generate income or serve a financial arrangement with another entity. Only narrow exceptions exist, dispatched by local authorities for transmission and distribution limits. Selling emergency-designated diesel as PJM capacity therefore likely requires reclassifying engines as non-emergency, which triggers stricter engine standards (Tier 4 or SCR-type controls), plus state NOx limits and possible major-source permitting. That is why the founder's 'retrofit the subset' step is likely the real cost and risk. It is also why incumbents have stayed away. The wedge exists only where the permit and retrofit math actually closes.

Other risks: PJM DR accreditation rules and limited-duration derating, which I could not verify because the PJM manual fetch returned only a table of contents. Local opposition to diesel. Hyperscalers and utilities choosing gas or battery capacity instead. | How this version avoids them: Voltus and CPower are dispatchers, and Voltus's Google deal covers batteries and thermostats, not generators or permits. They are conflicted as ledger-keepers and are natural certificate consumers, so we court them as design partners. ERock sells and operates its own gas hardware. OEM telemetry (Cat, Cummins and similar) is per-brand, not independent, and does not map runs to permit legal basis. DCIM and EHS software log air data but do not answer 'may I dispatch this engine now'. OpenADR and IEEE 2030.5 carry signals, not legality, so we build on them rather than compete. Trinity sells hourly permit projects, not a live neutral record, and could be a channel for onboarding. Note that the comparisons to OEM, DCIM and EHS vendors rest on my background knowledge, not verified this session.

title: The True Acceptance Map for Rural Transfers
one_liner: Voice AI agents call every receiving psychiatric unit and specialty hospital each night to learn what they will actually accept, and rural ERs text a number to find out who will say yes.
customer: Critical access hospital EDs, state hospital associations and state rural health offices (paid with Rural Health Transformation Program funds), and state behavioral health authorities. Subscription per hospital or per state.
problem: A rural ER holding a suicidal 16-year-old, or a stroke, trauma or OB patient, may spend 3-8 hours making phone calls to place them. State bed registries say beds are open, but the real decision is made by a house supervisor at 2am applying unwritten rules: no IV drug history, no one-to-one sitter, no autism, no patients over 250 lb, no out-of-state Medicaid, no aggression, and no calls after 9pm without a physician-to-physician call. Every ER charge nurse keeps a battered binder or a phone note of who says yes to what and who to ask for. It lives in one head, and it goes out of date when a house supervisor changes.
solution: Use voice agents to call each facility's intake line on a schedule and extract structured, current answers: true open capacity by population, unwritten exclusions, insurance rules, the name and direct number of the person who decides, and the hours that person answers. Serve it back through a plain SMS interface. A nurse texts 'psych, 16yo, Medicaid, sitter needed, hx cutting' and gets a ranked call list with the exact script to use (the words that get an acceptance). Only facility rules are collected. No patient data is ever in the calls. Later, sell a receiving-side listing so facilities can pre-qualify referrals and get fewer dead-end calls.
why_now: Every state has now posted Rural Health Transformation Program funding opportunities (as of August 2026), and care coordination and access technology are core uses. Research on bed-tracking systems shows registries still leave clinicians phoning to check appropriateness, especially for aggressive, medically complex, autistic and dementia patients. Voice agents from 2025-26 can now hold a natural two-minute call with an intake nurse for a few cents. The workforce shortage means intake lines are answered by fewer people, which makes the tacit rules more valuable.
revenue_model: $300-600 per ER per month for SMS access. State-level licenses of $100-300k per year paid from RHTP or behavioral health funds. A second line is a receiving-facility listing at about $500 per month per facility. The proprietary asset is a data graph of real rules that no registry has.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable data is not bed counts, which are wrong within an hour. It is the tacit acceptance criteria and the identity of the human who decides, and it can only be learned by phone at night. That is why bed-registry vendors (built on hospital self-reporting) miss it. Facilities that discover their rules are being published accurately will cooperate, because a dead-end call costs them time too.
first_30_days: Pick one state or region. Type up the founder nurse's own binder, about 60-80 facilities, into a spreadsheet. Wire an off-the-shelf voice agent platform to call each facility nightly and write results to a table. Put an SMS bot in front of it with a Twilio number. Give it free to five ERs in the region and compare call counts and time to placement before and after. Bring the numbers to the state hospital association and the RHTP office.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: OpenBeds (Bamboo Health, formerly Appriss Health), Behavioral Health Link (GCAL Real-Time Bed Registry and Crisis Now platform), State and hospital-association psychiatric bed registries (NC BH SCAN, WHA Psychiatric Bed Locator, Minnesota Bed Tracker, MABHA, Michigan registry dashboard), Human placement and crisis-access services (Illinois CARES Line, Massachusetts EPIA protocol, regional psychiatric emergency services, telepsychiatry vendors such as Array Behavioral Care and Access TeleCare). White space: Nobody found does the specific thing. Across roughly 20 searches, no startup, product, or open-source tool uses voice agents to phone receiving psychiatric units and specialty hospitals on a schedule and record their tacit acceptance rules, the name and hours of the decision-maker, and the script that works. The unserved wedge is real but narrow. (1) Registries (OpenBeds, BHL, state portals) capture bed counts and formal criteria through facility self-report. The 2019 ASPE and Psychiatric Services work found no state registry linked to EHR or ADT data, and respondents rated registry accuracy and timeliness poor. Only NC has hourly automation, and that is bed count, not rule extraction. (2) Nobody delivers a ranked call list plus script by SMS to a rural ER charge nurse. Registries are portals that still end in 'call the facility'. (3) The hardest-to-place groups are children, autism and IDD, aggression, medically complex, out-of-state Medicaid. Boarding research shows these patients wait longest, and generic registry filters handle them worst. (4) Decline reasons and real decision-makers are not aggregated across facilities anywhere. Not unserved: bed availability, digital referrals, and generic outbound voice AI. Also not a clean white space: stroke, trauma and OB, where hospital-run transfer centers and TeleTracking, Central Logic and RelateCare already own the workflow.

title: Commissioning Passport: The Data Center Readiness Standard
one_liner: Invert the model: the sponsor pays a neutral party to verify hall readiness once, in a machine-readable ledger every lender, insurer, landlord and offtaker can read, which grows into the standard definition of ready-for-service and the trigger written into loan, lease and backstop documents.
customer: Payers: sub-investment-grade neocloud sponsors and colocation developers, who face 4-6 counterparties each re-diligencing the same hall (issuer-pays). Readers who license access: lenders, DSU insurers, offtakers and backstop providers. Supply side, seeded free: commissioning agents, general contractors and IEs, who become named attestors.
problem: One liquid-cooled hall is diligenced repeatedly. The GPU-loan lender, the landlord's lender, the DSU insurer, the offtaker and any GPU-vendor backstop provider each hire their own advisor or IE, and evidence moves as emailed PDFs. Sponsors lose days on every draw and every counterparty re-asks the same questions. There is no shared definition of 'ready for service'. Lease commencement, financial close and backstop triggers can each key off a different milestone, and a backstop can lapse if construction runs more than about 180 days late. Because credibility is scarce, sponsors post letters of credit or parent guarantees, which is expensive capital to lock up.
solution: Two things. First, an open 'Readiness Ladder' spec, about 40 evidence-backed binary milestones for the last 90 days, published free so it can be adopted like a template. Second, the Passport ledger. Evidence is captured at source (Cx platform exports, utility letters, OEM startup bookings, CDU flush certificates, gear serial and bill-of-lading matches), timestamped and hashed, and tied to a named attestor (Cx agent, IE, OEM technician, utility). We add independent spot audits and a per-party permissioned view. Outputs are a Passport Score, a probability of RFS by date using reference-class priors, and a covenant schedule template (for example 'Ladder milestone L-7 certified in Passport') that counsel can drop into loan, lease and backstop documents so RFS is defined once. First product, sellable within 6 months, is the 'Draw Pack': within 5 business days of a draw or tranche request, we convert the sponsor's own commissioning evidence into a verified Passport snapshot that the lender has agreed to accept. It costs the sponsor $15K per pack or $8K/month per hall. Pilots go to sponsors that lenders cap, for whom verified readiness is a currency. The capture workspace is free for Cx agents and GCs, which seeds the supply side.
why_now: Lenders are capping neocloud exposure, deals are stalling on credit and some operators demand letters of credit or parent backing. Multi-party GPU structures with vendor backstops mean the same hall gets underwritten by many parties at once. The first-principles cost stack changed: turning IST results, punch lists and flush logs into structured pass/fail facts used to take a 3-person review team, and document AI now makes one reviewer per hall economically feasible. That makes portable verify-once evidence cheap enough to sell to the party that would otherwise pay for every counterparty's separate review. It would not have worked in 2019, when there was no GPU-debt market and no extraction tooling.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays verification at $15K per pack or $8-12K/month per hall. Read-side seats for lenders, insurers and offtakers at $40-150K per year, free for the first year to any lender that writes the Ladder into its documents. Licensed Passport Score and delivery-time benchmark indices for funds and reinsurers. Later, lenders offer margin step-downs or lower letter-of-credit haircuts for Passport-verified halls, and we take a fee from the sponsor's saving. Scale illustration: 150 halls under continuous verification at about $100K per year blended is about $15M revenue, with data licensing on top.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is a public good with a payer problem, and the answer is the one project-finance already uses. IEs are borrower-paid but lender-selected, and rating agencies are issuer-paid. The independence safeguards are a lender-vetoable attestor panel, published methodology and an audit trail. For the sponsor the product sells speed and a cheaper substitute for letters of credit and parent guarantees, not virtue. The moat is a cornered dataset: durations by OEM, utility, GC and hall type across every verified hall, which makes forecasts better as more halls join, so the network effect is in the prior. Counter-positioning also works: incumbents bill by the hour for each counterparty, and a portable verify-once artifact cannibalizes that repeat billing. The standard is won by whoever gets its definition of RFS into the legal templates first.
first_30_days: Publish Ladder spec v0.1 and teardowns of 2 publicly delayed projects, built from public documents. Recruit 4 Cx leads and one finance lawyer to draft the covenant schedule. Interview 15 sponsors and 10 lenders to measure which draw-package friction costs the most days and dollars. Sign 2 design partners: one sub-IG neocloud sponsor with a live delayed-draw facility, and its lender, who agrees in writing to accept the pack. Run the service by hand ('Wizard of Oz'): shared drive, spreadsheet and document-AI extraction, with no product build yet. Success by day 45: one lender accepts a Passport pack in place of a second-round advisor visit. Riskiest assumption to test first: sponsors will pay for verification that lenders accept, and lenders will accept sponsor-paid attestation. If not, fall back to Offspring 1 (lender-paid) and keep the ledger as a by-product.
lineage: mutation of I0365 ('Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. | How this version avoids them: Traditional IEs (Sargent & Lundy markets data center commissioning oversight and lender due diligence, so they are real incumbents): the Passport makes them attestors and partners, so they are a supply-side channel, not a rival. This also blunts the incumbent-adds-a-service-line risk, because their work becomes an input to our ledger. SynMax/IIR, Epoch, Currence: exterior and desk data, taken as inputs and potential co-marketing or referral partners. SemiAnalysis: paid research and ratings-style brands for neocloud operations, not hall-level evidence, and possibly a distribution partner for the index. Peony: a data-room vendor for fleet and telemetry files that could add a Cx module, so it is the closest emerging rival to watch, or an integration partner. Uptime Tier: a one-time end-of-build certificate on design and performance, not a continuous last-90-days schedule ledger. Risks I could not verify: whether lenders will accept issuer-paid evidence, and whether an established engineering firm would launch a competing 'portable' standard once the concept is visible. Publishing the spec early and embedding it in legal templates is the defense.

title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Pitch three mid-size dating, gig or cannabis-tech platforms and one cyber MGA. Offer a free 90-day pilot against one vendor under NDA. Publish an anonymised benchmark from the pilot to generate inbound.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Vanta (compliance automation), SecurityScorecard, Transcend (privacy/DSR orchestration), Age Check Certification Scheme (ACCS) and Age Verification Providers Association (AVPA) standards ecosystem. White space: Research limits first. WebSearch hit its 200-call session cap before I could run any of the planned startup, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt searches, so I did not verify the absence of a direct startup. I used WebFetch on named pages and GitHub repo searches instead. Wikipedia and vendor-site fetches turned up no company that recruits real, consenting individuals, enrols them in a platform's live ID or age-check flow, files deletion and access requests with the vendor and its sub-processors, watches for the canary strings, and issues an attestation. GitHub searches for open-source tools returned nothing relevant.

What is unserved: outcome-based, adversarial proof of the promise to forget. Incumbents cover the adjacent layers.
- Compliance automation (Vanta) covers whether controls exist on paper.
- Standards bodies (ACCS, Kantara, AVPA/ISO 27566) cover process and control audits.
- SecurityScorecard covers passive outside-in ratings.
- DSR orchestration (Transcend) covers a customer's own deletions.
- Honeytoken vendors cover a customer's own intrusions.
- HIBP-style monitors cover leaked-string detection.

The specific unserved piece is an independent, real-human, live-flow test with a public per-vendor retention benchmark.

Structural weaknesses of the pitch:
- Real government ID numbers cannot be unique canaries. Only emails, phones, addresses and name variants are. Leak detection depends on those fields surfacing in dumps, and image-only dumps are hard to search.
- The base rate of any given vendor leaking in a quarter is low. Most attestations would say nothing found, which is weak evidence. Retention and deletion behaviour, tested through DSARs and access requests, is the part canaries can actually prove.
- Vendors may treat the enrolments as terms-of-service violations. Customer consent helps but does not remove that risk.
- Privacy-preserving designs such as on-device age estimation and reusable digital ID could shrink the retention problem that this idea audits.

title: Section 8 Rent-Increase Deadline Capture Service
one_liner: A tracker that knows each voucher tenant's lease anniversary, sees the new FY2027 payment standard, and files the landlord's rent-increase request inside the tight 60-day window before a year of raise is forfeited.
customer: Small landlords with 1 to 50 Housing Choice Voucher units, especially out-of-state investors in Section 8-heavy markets such as Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Small PM firms with voucher portfolios are the second segment.
problem: Housing-authority payment standards rose for FY2027, but a new standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1. It applies only at each tenant's lease anniversary. The owner must send a written request within a typically tight window, often 60 days before that date, or forfeit the increase for a year. Each housing authority has its own forms and dates. Most small owners never map the anniversary dates, so they leave real money uncollected. One market analysis found 3-bedroom increases of 6 to 12%, with a median of 10%.
solution: The landlord uploads photos of their HAP contracts and leases, and the tool extracts tenant anniversary dates and current contract rents. The team maintains a database of housing-authority payment standards and each authority's request process (scraped from PHA PDFs and notices, human-verified). For each unit it computes the increase headroom, alerts at 90, 75 and 60 days before the window closes, and generates the authority-specific rent-increase request letter or form. It tracks proof of submission and logs who was contacted and when. It also flags likely mistakes in the original rent-reasonableness record (wrong bedroom count or square footage) that justify a correction request mid-lease.
why_now: FY2027 standards take effect around October 1, 2026, and today is 2026-09-28. Anniversary windows are opening across the country right now. The forum thread on this appeared within days, and the one-year forfeiture is a hard deadline that makes people spend money.
revenue_model: Success-aligned pricing: $5 per unit per month, plus 1 month of the captured increase for each unit where the request is approved. On a $1,300 rent and a 10% bump, that is $130 per month, or $1,560 a year, per unit. Authority data is the moat; a PM-firm plan can charge per door. Later, a similar deadline tracker can cover annual recertification and inspection dates.
non_obvious_insight: The money is lost to a calendar, not to the tenant or the market, and the people who feel it are the least likely to be organized. A BiggerPockets post titled 'Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it' says: 'A new payment standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1'. It adds that owners must submit written requests within a typically tight 60-day window before each anniversary or forfeit the opportunity for an entire year. It reports 3-bedroom rates up 6-12% (median 10%) in nine of ten low-cost ZIP codes, and notes that St. Louis adopted its FY2027 standards effective Jan 1, 2027 (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Out-of-state voucher landlords also struggle with local rules, as in a Cleveland thread on Section 8 inspection standards (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection). A separate thread notes Section 8 tenants are 'already at maximum allowable rates' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants).
first_30_days: Week 1: hand-build payment-standard tables and request procedures for 3 housing authorities (start with St. Louis, Cleveland and Memphis). Publish a free calculator, 'How much did you leave on the table this year?', in the BiggerPockets Out-of-State and Landlording forums. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 15 landlords, send requests manually with the templates, and track approvals. Week 4: turn on success-fee billing, and pitch 3 small voucher-heavy PM firms. Target: 15 landlords, 100+ units, and 10 documented approved increases.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: RentsPaid, HAPSecure, TenantKeep, VoucherReady. White space: The reminder and calendar layer is not open. RentsPaid, HAPSecure and TenantKeep already ship anniversary or rent-increase-window alerts at free to $39/mo, and TenantKeep advertises PHA letter generation. A plain tracker with alerts would be a fourth entrant selling against free. All of them are software-only and unfunded. What remains unserved is (1) actually filing the request and chasing it to approval, since TenantKeep says outright that it does not file; (2) a human-verified, authority-by-authority rulebook (window length, form, portal versus mail, comps requirement, tenant signature) in the Section 8-heavy investor markets: Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis, Indianapolis; VoucherReady explicitly declines to supply PHA numbers; (3) contingency pricing tied to captured increase, when every competitor charges flat SaaS or free; (4) a portfolio leakage audit for small PM firms and out-of-state investors (units at or under the new payment standard with no filed request). Two caveats. Payment standard increases apply to the family's subsidy at the next regular reexam (24 CFR 982.505), not at the lease anniversary, so the pitch conflates two clocks. Rent reasonableness also caps the gain, and BiggerPockets commenters note many voucher units are already at the local maximum.

title: Plumber Parts Ledger: Margin Recovery Plus Failure Evidence
one_liner: Give plumbing shops a free contingency audit of unbilled parts, and pay them a bounty to bag failed pipes and fittings. The invoices become the installed-base denominator that makes the failure evidence valuable to insurers and manufacturers.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops ($1.5-15M revenue, 5-40 techs) as the supply side. Paying buyers are regional and mutual homeowners insurers' subrogation units and subro vendors, plumbing manufacturers and private-label buyers, and later distributors.
problem: Shops leak margin on parts bought but never billed. Plumbers also throw away the failed supply line or fitting that would have made a $9k water loss recoverable, because nobody pays them the four minutes it takes to bag it. Failure counts alone are weak, since manufacturers' lawyers can dismiss them without knowing how many units were sold, installed and stayed fine.
solution: Shops forward supply-house invoices and give a field-service export. An LLM parser ties invoice lines to jobs and returns a weekly leak list, paid at 25% of recovered revenue, with no fee if nothing is found. The same app hands out tamper-evident QR bags. A 90-second phone flow captures photo in place, date code, homeowner e-signature and claim number, and a weekly courier pickup delivers chain-of-custody parts. Each bag is auto-linked to the job's SKU, install date and installer from the invoice ledger. Outputs are subrogation evidence packs, per-SKU failure-rate reports (failures per 10,000 units sold), and at-risk-address lists for proactive replacement.
why_now: Water damage is one of the top two homeowner claim categories, and insurers are squeezed enough that routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. LLM invoice parsing now works on messy supply-house PDFs and photos, which made both products cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for 12 months, converting to $199-499 per month monitoring. $75-150 per bagged part from insurers or subro vendors (of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech), plus a 3-8% success share on recoveries. $15-60k per year failure-data licenses to manufacturers and distributors. Later, per-address replacement programs sold to insurers as loss prevention.
non_obvious_insight: The denominator only exists in the shop's invoices, and it arrives as a byproduct of margin recovery. It converts anecdotes into rates manufacturers can't wave away. It also identifies who installed which SKU at which address and when, which decides warranty windows and statute of repose. The installed-base list is the real prize: when a lot goes bad, the insurer can pay $15 to replace a braided line at every address that received it, instead of paying $9k after it bursts.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and owner peer groups with a free 90-day audit and a free evidence kit. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number. Pay a flat $50 per bag and collect the first 50 parts with photos. Link each part to its invoice line. Take 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subro vendor and sell a 100-part paid pilot.
lineage: hybrid of I0689 + I0068 (Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation + Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials). Why stronger: The audit alone is a crowded, ServiceTitan-adjacent feature with thin defensibility. The bounty alone has a cold-start problem: shops have no reason to stay engaged and the data has no denominator. Together, the free audit is the near-zero-CAC hook into the same shops, the bounty gives them a second paycheck, and the joined install-and-failure ledger is a dataset neither ServiceTitan nor a forensic firm can assemble.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Donan Engineering - Loss Logistics, Envista Forensics and Rimkus (forensic engineering / property loss consulting), LeakBot, ServiceTitan and CompanyCam (plumber field software). White space: Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) before any search ran. This verdict rests on direct page fetches of about a dozen vendor, industry and government sites, plus two empty GitHub searches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or trade press, so I could not rule out a small funded startup doing exactly this. Run 4-6 searches before committing money. Suggested queries: 'subrogation evidence preservation plumber', 'failed part bounty', 'water loss evidence kit', and the same on Crunchbase.

What I found is a real gap in what I could reach. Evidence logistics and forensic engineering exist for engineer-assigned losses (Donan, Envista, Rimkus). Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). No page I read describes any of these paying or equipping the plumber to retain the failed part on routine sub-$15k water losses. The public failure data I found is weak (SaferProducts.gov). Nothing I found is a date-code and brand-level failure-rate dataset.

Unserved specifically: (1) plumber-side capture at the moment of removal, including a per-part payment. (2) A neutral custodian and evidence package for the $8-15k tier, which is below the point where a $2k engineer is dispatched. (3) A structured brand, model and date-code failure dataset from real removed parts.

The main risks are structural, not competitive. (a) The plumber often arrives before a claim exists, so the claim number and the bounty payer are unknown at bagging. (b) Mitigation contractors and insurer-dispatched vendors may reach the site first on many losses. (c) The recovery economics of small product-defect claims are unproven, so insurers may not pay $75-150 for parts they would not pursue anyway. (d) A public brand-level failure report invites manufacturer legal pushback. (e) A 'cause-of-loss statement' from a tech risks unlicensed-engineering objections. (f) I could not fetch HomeServe (403), so I cannot say whether that plumber-network incumbent already does something like this. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces.

title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). White space: Nobody offers flat-fee coverage of 15-minute California family-law hearings. That is because the core mechanic, private reporters dialing in from anywhere, is currently barred. Gov. Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). San Diego's court page states 'the court is prohibited by law from allowing remote court reporting for any court proceeding' (https://sdcourt.ca.gov/sdcourt/generalinformation/resourcelists/courtreporterinformation). The idea's claim that AB 3013 'opened remote reporting' to a private platform is wrong. Unserved and still legal: (1) physical-presence short-hearing coverage, where one pro tem covers several departments in the same courthouse using calendar-based duration prediction, and no vendor markets a per-hearing SKU; (2) a scheduling and utilization layer sold to courts to fill pro tem and official reporter slots, aimed at hiring and retention (the ruling names 'pro tem reporters paid by the court' as a compliance route, and court reporter counsel is calling on courts to lift hiring freezes); (3) fast certified transcripts of court electronic recordings for attorneys who need appellate-grade records. The white space is real but is a legal-regime bet on remote reporting being opened to private reporters, plus a narrow physical-hopping wedge. It is not a software-only wedge. Court reporter unions opposed AB 3013 and are a political headwind.

title: Human Bench Network for AI Agents
one_liner: An API-fronted network of laid-off expert bench scientists who run ad hoc wet-lab experiments for AI agents and return machine-readable execution records.
customer: AI-first biotechs, AI-for-science startups and university groups (5-60 people, seed to Series B) that run agent swarms but have no wet lab; later, programs adjacent to frontier labs.
problem: Agent swarms now propose far more experiments than anyone can run. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates using ~950 agents in 21 hours. Stanford's Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents, Science, Sept 17, 2026) says the next step is testing findings in real labs. Cloud labs and robots handle fixed assays, but not ad hoc molecular biology: Anthropic itself found robotics less conducive to ad hoc workflows and kept human scientists at the bench. Human review and bench work are the bottleneck.
solution: Ticketed experiments through an API or MCP endpoint. The agent proposes a protocol and a senior scientist does feasibility triage. A vetted contractor then runs it at sublet or surplus benches, BSL-1/2 only. Each job returns a signed record that separates AI proposal, human edit and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). Fixed price per experiment. Start with commodity molecular biology: cloning, small-scale expression and purification, ELISA/BLI/qPCR, enzyme activity, bacterial and cell-culture assays.
why_now: Frontier labs and Stanford now say publicly that bench execution is the bottleneck. BioSpace tracks 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies in 2026, which supplies skilled hands. The OpenAI Foundation plans to distribute $1B by year-end through Public Data for Health, which creates grant-funded demand for data generation. Lab Manager notes there is no sign-off standard for AI-directed experiments, and this record format supplies one. Anthropic has said it wants to work with other scientists.
revenue_model: $1.5-8k per experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, monthly retainers with minimum volumes for agent-heavy customers, and a premium for 48-hour turnaround. The platform keeps a take rate on contractor labor.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is now nearly free compared with bench throughput, and robots failed as the universal answer because real biology is ad hoc. The defensible assets are a pre-vetted pool of humans and a structured execution record that agents can learn from. Humans become the last-mile actuator for AI. Adaptyv and cloud labs cover single fixed assays; nobody sells the long tail of one-off experiments.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 laid-off molecular biologists in Boston, SF and San Diego through layoff trackers and alumni groups. Rent 2-3 sublet benches or surplus CRO benches. Define three ticket types with fixed prices. Pitch 10 AI protein-design and agent startups and close 3-5 pilots. Aim for the first 20 paid experiments and publish the sample record schema.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems), Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints), Emerald Cloud Lab, Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces). White space: Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).
- Sublet-bench operations carry insurance, contamination, quality-control and IP-chain-of-custody risk that a software-style API hides.
- The 35-45% gross margin at $1.5-8k per experiment is unproven against commodity CROs and against Adaptyv's automation, which starts at $149 per protein for screening-level binding.

title: Federal-Agreement Lab for State SNAP QC Reviewers
one_liner: Sell calibration drills to the small, high-leverage group whose findings set the official error rate, the state QC reviewers, scoring them against a federal answer key and putting part of the fee at risk on the state-federal disagreement rate.
customer: State SNAP Quality Control unit directors and the state SNAP directors who sponsor them, in the 41 states above 6% that must now file remediation plans. Each QC unit is a few dozen reviewers. Warm lead: Alabama DHR, which posted an RFP for 'SNAP Quality Control review assessment and training'. Check who won and at what scope. Targets: states within about 1 point of a tier line, once the FY2025 state table is pulled.
problem: The official rate is not the state's own number. USDA re-reviews a subsample and adjusts (regresses) the state's findings, and disputed differences go to arbitration. Rates are cliffs (6/8/10%), each worth tens to hundreds of millions in state benefit cost. A state QC reviewer who under-calls errors gets corrected upward by federal re-review. One who over-calls inflates the state's own rate. QC units are small and turnover-prone, and the FNS 310 handbook is dense. Today that calibration happens ad hoc, in meetings or through occasional consultants.
solution: A library of about 200 synthetic completed-review packets: case file, interview notes and an 'as-reviewed' finding, with planted misses and planted false alarms. Answer keys are adjudicated by retired FNS and state reviewers and cite FNS 310 sections. Reviewers find the errors, and we score agreement with the key by element (income, household composition, shelter, resources, ABAWD/H.R.1 rules), by reviewer and by supervisor. We add weekly live calibration sessions run by the retired reviewers, and an arbitration-readiness checklist. We do not perform QC reviews. We train and score, which keeps us clear of the federal oversight rules for third-party QC contractors (verify against the 2018 Farm Bill provisions). Method is symmetric: the goal is agreement with the federal standard, not lower error counts.
why_now: FY2025 rates came out June 24, 2026: 41 states above 6% and a 10.62% national rate. FY2026 rates finalize through federal re-review and arbitration into mid-2027, and states can use the better of FY2025 and FY2026 for FY2028. The FY2027 sample opens Oct 1, 2026 and sets FY2030 cost share. H.R.1 made every QC finding a budget line, so QC directors now have executive attention and remediation-plan deadlines. The Alabama RFP shows states already buy QC-side assessment and training.
revenue_model: $90-250k per state QC unit per year: about $2.5-4k per reviewer seat, a packet-library license and quarterly calibration sessions. 20-25% of the fee is at risk, refunded if the state-federal difference rate on FNS re-reviewed cases does not narrow. FNS measures that outcome, not us. 41 states at 40% penetration is about $5-8M ARR, so the ceiling is small but each logo is high-value and fast to close. Expansion: Medicaid eligibility-error programs (H.R.1 adds payment reductions starting around FY2030, verify), plus a per-case add-on for arbitration memo review. Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dollars at stake per trained head is 100-1000x higher for QC reviewers than for eligibility workers. A 30-person unit's calibration can swing a tier cliff worth $100M+, and a county worker's cannot. The regressed rate turns under-calling into a hidden tax, not good luck. Unlike eligibility policy, which varies by state, QC review method is national (FNS 310), so one packet library serves every state. That fixes the parent's per-state case-library cost problem. The buyer population is tiny, homogeneous and reachable through a few networks.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: pull the Alabama RFP, announcement and results documents to learn the winner, scope and price. Recruit 2 retired state or FNS QC reviewers as adjudicators at $100-150 an hour. Days 5-18: write 25 planted-error packets from the public FNS 310 handbook and published arbitration guidance. Days 10-30: reach 15 QC directors through APHSA payment-accuracy contacts and FNS regional liaisons. Offer a free blind 10-packet test for 5 of their reviewers and return an agreement-gap report within a week. Convert 1-2 to $25-40k pilots via simplified procurement.

The Alabama RFP winner is the one real competitor to profile in week one.

title: Escrow and Assay Settlement House for Scrap
one_liner: A neutral settlement house that holds the buyer's money in a licensed escrow and the sealed sample in a vault, then releases payment automatically on the assay of record. It starts with black mass and grows into a registry, financing and an index.
customer: Two sides. Sellers are mid-size dismantlers and pre-processors who fear both assay games and recycler insolvency after the 2025 restructurings. Buyers are recyclers who want to win feed, especially weakly capitalised or new-capacity ones that can rent credibility from a neutral escrow. The first anchor is one buyer signing our Standard Settlement Terms, which opens every one of its sellers at once. A buyer pays half the fee.
problem: The parent sells arbitration after the fight, once, to a price-sensitive party in trouble. Sellers actually face two bundled anxieties on every lot. One is assay noise or bias. The other is credit exposure on the assay-based final payment, unsecured for weeks and frozen if the lot is disputed. After Li-Cycle's sale to Glencore and other 2025 restructurings, sellers price that risk by discounting or refusing weaker buyers. Nobody sells both fixes in one contract. Banks' letters of credit and provisional payments cover part of the credit side, and assay disputes are left to umpire clauses.
solution: Sold within six months as a Settle-in-14-days contract pack. It is a tri-party agreement (buyer, seller, us) drafted once by a trade-finance law firm. A licensed escrow agent or bank partner holds funds, and we never hold money or inventory. A certified crew takes a sealed triplicate sample-of-record at the seller's dock. One split goes to a pre-agreed accredited lab, and two are stored in a third-party vault. Payment releases by formula, payable times assay-of-record, with no ex-post negotiation. Only if the retained splits differ beyond the pre-agreed Gy variance tolerance is the third split assayed. Later layers are these. (1) An accreditation programme so inspection companies' and recyclers' crews sample under our protocol and pay a licence, so the majors distribute us. (2) A lot registry whose receipts lenders advance 85-90% against, for an origination share. (3) An assay-consistent payables index sold to price reporting agencies. (4) Extension to e-scrap boards, catalyst scrap, mixed copper and Ni/Co intermediates.
why_now: Counterparty fear is at a high after the 2025 restructurings, and buyers need a way to attract supply. Black mass flows are being channelled into a bounded, regulated EU/OECD corridor, so a few dozen counterparties and a few hundred lanes can be covered by one house. Escrow and instant-payment rails, e-signature and vault-and-hash registries are now commodity. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 already forces lot-level composition records that the registry can generate.
revenue_model: A take rate of 0.8-1.2% of lot value split between buyer and seller (EUR 1-1.8k on a EUR 150k lot). A pass-through crew fee of EUR 600-900. Small float income. A 0.3-0.5% lender origination share once receipts are financeable. Accreditation licences. Bottom-up: if European black mass trades EUR 0.5-1.5B a year (an estimate, unverified), 1% on a third of it is EUR 2-5M a year before scrap classes beyond black mass. The scale story is the registry and standard, with the lender and index revenue on top. It is a settlement network with float, not a lab.
non_obvious_insight: Inversion: buyers and sellers do not need a smarter referee, they need the decision made before the dispute. Moving the assay of record from ex-post arbitration to an ex-ante release trigger converts a service sold once, in trouble, into infrastructure sold on every lot with a take on GMV. The most credit-challenged recycler is the natural first buyer, because a neutral escrow lets it rent credibility, so the expected resistor is the first to sign. Independence stays the asset, because only a party that neither samples for a side nor holds inventory can be the registry.
first_30_days: Draft the tri-party terms with a trade-finance law firm (about EUR 8-15k) and shortlist two escrow or bank partners. Pitch five recyclers, prioritising new capacity or weak balance sheets, on being the anchor buyer for Standard Settlement Terms. Pitch the three sellers from the audit funnel. Target one signed letter of intent from a buyer and three escrowed lots at half fee by month 4. Check whether digital metals trading platforms such as Metalshub already run escrow plus assay for black mass, which I could not verify. Also test with one lender whether a certified lot receipt would raise their advance rate.

title: Handoff Assay of Record for EU Recyclers
one_liner: A co-signed black mass assay with a stated uncertainty at each handoff from a first recycler to a hydromet plant, so both sides' EU Battery Regulation mass balances close. The regulated first recycler pays, on a compliance budget, not the seller in a settlement fight.
customer: First recyclers, meaning mechanical pre-processors that shred cells and modules and ship black mass on to hydromet. About 25-40 sites across the EU are in scope. The economic buyer is the head of compliance/EHS or the CFO. Secondary payers are the hydromet recycler, which co-pays for the input documentation it needs, and extended-producer-responsibility organisations that audit recycling chains.
problem: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 sets the calculation and verification methodology for recycling efficiency and material recovery. It was verified this session as in force from 24 July 2025, with annual data submission to the member-state authority from 2026 and first material-recovery targets due 31 December 2027. Secondary sources say it requires a mass balance of input, intermediate and output fractions with composition data, that black mass is an intermediate fraction, and that the first recycler must coordinate data across downstream treatment. Those points are not verified against the act text, and how input composition must be determined is unknown. Black mass therefore sits exactly at the joint. The pre-processor reports what it sent on, using its dispatch assay, and the hydromet reports what it received, using its receipt assay. When the two assays of the same lot differ by 5-15%, the chain shows phantom Co/Ni/Li losses or gains. The first recycler is blamed either way and cannot show whether it clears a recovery target.
solution: A Handoff Certificate per lot. A sealed sample-of-record is co-signed by both sites and assayed once by an accredited lab under a Gy-based protocol, with declared moisture basis and a stated sampling-variance component. Both sites use that single number. On top sits a Chain Reconciler, a small web tool. It ingests certificates plus mass and yield data, propagates the sampling variance through the delegated act's formulas by Monte Carlo, and outputs the documentation-format annual report. Recovery rates carry confidence intervals, for example 'Co recovery 91.3% plus or minus 3.1%, provably above target' or 'cannot demonstrate compliance'. The stage-1 recycler pays a certificate fee of EUR 350-700 per lot plus a EUR 25-60k annual site subscription. Stage-2 co-signs and pays a smaller receipt-side fee. Verifiers and PROs buy audit packs. Sampling is done by contracted crews with portable kits, so there is no station capex.
why_now: The first annual reporting cycle under the 2025 methodology is live in 2026, and the first 2027 recovery targets are 15 months out. That is when recyclers discover their handoff numbers do not reconcile. The methodology was only fixed in mid-2025, so any tool built for it is new. Black mass has also become a controlled, largely within-OECD flow (a secondary source cites Basel Annex VIII export limits), which makes a small, identifiable set of handoffs.
revenue_model: Subscription plus usage. Per-site ACV of EUR 40-90k for stage-1 sites, with lot certificates included up to a tier. Stage-2 receipt-side fees. PRO and verifier audit packs of EUR 20-50k. Ceiling of roughly EUR 1.2-2.7M ARR from 30 EU stage-1 sites, and more from hydromet co-pay and PRO packs. Later, recycled-content documentation for cell makers and OEMs, which phases in from about 2028 and needs verification, becomes a second, larger payer.
non_obvious_insight: The customer is not buying accuracy but consistency and a defensible uncertainty. For a regulator's mass balance, it matters more that both ends of a handoff quote the same number with a stated variance than that the number is perfect. A recycler at 91% against a 90% target cannot claim compliance without an uncertainty statement, and with one it can. The compliance owner has a different budget from commercial procurement, does not haggle over EUR 500 a lot, and prefers to have a third party on record. It is the same sampling insight, sold as risk cover instead of dispute settlement.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: read the delegated act's annexes and documentation template to confirm how input and intermediate composition is sourced, and kill or reshape the idea if it just accepts supplier-declared values. Days 5-20: ask 8 first recyclers for 12 months of black mass dispatch assays and hydromet receipt assays (both are on settlement statements). Run a free one-page Chain Gap Check that translates the assay gap into percentage points of reported Co/Ni/Li recovery. Days 20-30: convert 2-3 to six-month certificate pilots, and open talks with one environmental verifier or consultancy that would carry the Reconciler into its verification engagements.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SGS (independent inspection, sampling and assay), Bureau Veritas / Inspectorate (commodities inspection), Intertek (Caleb Brett / minerals and battery testing), Alex Stewart International. White space: Provisional, because the research was severely constrained: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any search ran, and the direct fetches of incumbent sites returned 403, 404 or no relevant content.
