title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history.

title: Scribe-Adjusted EBITDA: Privileged Diligence for Physician Deals
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day, counsel-engaged report that tells private equity buyers how much of a scribe-enabled physician group's revenue is real, and what the rest could cost them.
customer: Deal partners and VPs at lower-middle-market PE funds and MSOs buying 20-150 provider specialty groups (dermatology, orthopedics, ophthalmology, GI, urology, behavioral health, primary care) that adopted an ambient scribe in the last 18 months. The engaging party is the buyer's healthcare transactions counsel, so the work is privileged. Quality-of-earnings accounting firms are channel partners, not rivals.
problem: Buyers pay a multiple of EBITDA that now includes scribe-era E/M uplift, and drift dollars fall through at near-100% margin. Illustration (assumptions to validate): $30M revenue, 40% E/M, 6% scribe uplift gives $0.72M, about 14% of a $5M EBITDA, or roughly $8M of enterprise value at 11x. A stock deal also inherits overpayment liability, and the 60-day return rule starts once a problem is identified. Nobody in the deal team can answer the question. QoE accountants have no coder bench. Regulatory counsel runs generic billing samples. Seller materials and scribe vendor 'AAPC-verified' claims are self-serving. The parent's own research flags that the drift may be legitimate documentation catch-up, so buyers cannot tell whether to discount it or trust it.
solution: Deliverable is a 'Scribe-Adjusted Run-Rate Report', engaged through deal counsel under a privilege-preserving engagement letter. (1) Causal drift estimate: 24-36 months of claims from the data room plus each provider's scribe go-live date from the seller's admin console. Because rollouts are staggered, non-adopters and late adopters in the same group form a built-in control group, so a staggered difference-in-differences replaces a naive before/after. (2) Coder-signed sample: 150-300 stratified encounters from the highest-drift providers, reviewed by certified coders on MDM and time statements. This splits drift into 'supported catch-up' and 'at-risk narration'. (3) Outputs: a scribe-adjusted EBITDA range, an extrapolated overpayment exposure with a confidence interval, and recommended escrow, specific indemnity or price adjustment language. It also includes a 100-day post-close remediation and refund plan. (4) Later: the same report sold sell-side ('prove your uplift is clean before you go to market') to cut re-trades.
why_now: Scribes went mainstream across groups in 2025-26, so the first wave of PE deals with 12-24 months of scribe-era claims is closing now. Payers have begun automated E/M downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025 is reported), so uplift in the trailing run-rate may not persist. The FCA enforcement climate makes successor liability a live diligence topic. There is no historical playbook, because this diligence item did not exist in 2023.
revenue_model: $20-45k per buy-side report, priced by provider count and data volume. $8-15k for a sell-side readiness version. Optional 100-day post-close monitor at $4-8k per month. Direct cost is roughly $3-5k per report (30-45 coder hours plus senior review), so gross margin is about 80%. Two people can deliver one to two reports a week. A benchmark subscription for funds is a later add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Two things. First, the buyer does not need the scribe to be wrong. They need a number, and the staggered rollout gives each target its own control group, which the drift studies with pre/post design and the free-diagnostic framing in the parent both miss. Second, EBITDA leverage makes a $30k report protect about $8M of price, so it is priced against the deal, not against a compliance budget. The same report is also valuable to a seller with clean documentation, which makes it a two-sided product that gets better as deals accumulate.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build a public-data pre-screen from the CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service file (updated May 2026). It shows each NPI's E/M level mix by year for any target roster. Public data means no client claims and no privilege problem, but the year lag means it only catches early adopters, so the full report needs data-room claims. Retain a healthcare regulatory attorney to draft the privileged engagement template, and contract 2 CPC/CPMA coders. Days 8-30: contact 25 healthcare-transactions lawyers at mid-market firms and 20 lower-middle-market PE healthcare associates, offering a free public-data pre-screen on any target they are bidding on under NDA. Aim for one paid confirmatory-diligence pilot at $12-15k, in exchange for the right to keep de-identified aggregate statistics and a reference.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: VMG Health is the incumbent most able to copy this, because it does transaction-side valuation and compliance work. The defense is packaging, not technology: a narrow fixed-price 10-day product built around a causal design, delivered through deal counsel, plus a deal-by-deal benchmark of typical uplift by scribe vendor and specialty that grows with each engagement. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer, MDaudit and Healthicity are software sold to a practice's in-house compliance team on an annual cycle. In diligence the practice is the seller, so the buyer is different and the clock is different. Scribe vendors (Ambience, Abridge, DeepScribe) and autonomous coders (Fathom, Arintra, CodaMetrix) self-attest, so a buyer cannot rely on them. Trilliant and BCBSA publish the drift and define what a payer will challenge, but neither sells a per-target answer. Our report resolves the 'may be legitimate documentation catch-up' caveat that Trilliant itself raises.

title: Dark Roof Capital: Buy, Cure, Re-Perform
one_liner: Invert the parent. Instead of being paid a $3k fee to cure other people's stranded solar loans, buy those loans at dark-roof prices, finish the systems with a proprietary per-AHJ cure playbook, and keep the full value uplift as a re-performing loan pool.
customer: Sellers: credit unions, banks, servicers and ABS trusts or controlling-class holders that want dark and forbearance-stuck solar loans off their books. Capital side: distressed-credit funds, family offices and NPL buyers who want a new niche but cannot cure a roof. Homeowners are offered a cure and a payment reset in exchange for reinstating payments.
problem: Dark solar loans are an orphan asset class with broken pricing. NPL desks discount them to zero collateral value because they cannot fix the system. Lenders will not cure at scale and cannot collect on a roof that produces nothing. A cure costs perhaps 10-15% of the loan balance yet restores most of its value, but a $3k cure fee captures only about 10% of the $20k+ of value created. The holder of the loan keeps 90%, and today nobody who can cure holds the loan.
solution: Use the forensic pack from the parent as an underwriting engine. Sell a Bid Desk: audit a seller's dark loans, then quote a purchase price within 10 days. First 6 months: sell a zero-upfront cure-share product to a credit union (we finish the jobs, and take about 25% of restored loan value once PTO is achieved and payments resume), funded by a small working-capital line. Then buy pools through an SPV with a licensed sub-servicer. Cure with the playbook and offer borrowers a reset (a rate or principal modification in exchange for reinstatement). Hold or resell re-performing pools. Longer term, securitize re-performing solar loans, as mortgage RPL funds do. Purchases are limited to loans where the borrower is engaged and in forbearance, with reps and warranties and a seller-funded holdback for claims.
why_now: Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower and PosiGen mean a growing pool of dark loans now exists, with forbearance windows expiring. Post-25D, lenders are shifting from origination to workout and want clean books. Mortgage NPL and RPL buyers already exist and are looking for new asset classes in a higher-rate world. Cheap agentic records recovery makes the per-loan diligence cost low enough to bid on small-balance loans.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (0-6 months): cure-share, about 25% of restored loan value, with zero upfront cost to the seller. Phase 2: spread on purchased loans. Illustration only: buy a $35k loan at about $11k (roughly 32% of balance), spend about $3.5k to cure, and a re-performing loan is worth about $24-28k, giving a $10-13k gross uplift before servicing, legal and default haircuts. Investors in the SPV pay roughly a 1.5% management fee and 20% carry above an 8% preferred return. The operating company also earns cure and coordination fees. Phase 3: RPL securitization fees.
non_obvious_insight: Fee-for-service captures the wrong slice of value, and whoever can cure at the lowest cost can bid the highest and still make money. Pure NPL funds cannot cure, lenders will not, and cure contractors have no balance sheet, so the buyer with the best per-AHJ playbook has a structural cost advantage. Dark solar loans also carry a specific hidden liability for buyers. Under the FTC Holder Rule, a homeowner can raise installer misconduct claims against whoever holds the loan. Curing the system removes the basis for most of those claims, so the cure is also the de-risking step, and buyers who cannot cure are pricing that risk at its maximum.
first_30_days: Use the audit engine to build a bid model on 50-100 loans from a friendly credit union or servicer under NDA, and price them. Get a commitment letter from one distressed-credit family office for a $1-2M first-loss pilot. Commission a legal memo on the Holder Rule, state lender and servicer licensing, and rescission risk, and identify a licensed sub-servicer. Sign one cure-share deal (no purchase) covering about 30 loans to measure real cure cost per tier and how many borrowers reinstate. Write a one-page pool teaser for investors. The riskiest assumption is borrower willingness to resume payments and rescission exposure, so measure reinstatement rates before buying anything.

Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). title: Independent Audit Samples for Modeled Lead Inventories
one_liner: Become the independent auditor of predictive lead-line inventories: sell engineering consultants and state reviewers a statistically designed sample of 60-150 photo-verified lines that proves a model's error rate, paid per ground-truth point plus an annual attestation fee.
customer: Regional engineering and environmental consulting firms (50-500 staff) that win lead-line inventory work as prime contractor, license or run a predictive model, and must defend the classification to a state reviewer. Wedge: firms holding three or more utility inventory contracts in a state whose drinking-water program requires field validation of modeled non-lead classifications, or in a state that rejects pure modeling (Texas is reported not to accept predictive modeling for official inventories, verify before selling). The state reviewer is the second beneficiary, and the utility is the eventual budget owner.
problem: Predictive modelers and consultants classify tens of thousands of unknown lines statistically, but a regulator or council will ask 'what is your error rate?' The consultant's current answer is a field crew, a subcontractor or potholing, priced at hundreds of dollars per point, with no independence from the party selling the model. Vendors that sell both prediction and verification are grading their own homework. In the parent idea the buyer was a utility that needed tens of thousands of lines cleared, which made low homeowner response and thin supply fatal. An audit needs far fewer points.
solution: An audit-sample service. We draw a stratified random sample from the utility's modeled bins (predicted non-lead, predicted lead, low-confidence), so the sample design is ours and can't be steered by the modeler. Homeowners get a utility-letterhead notice with a $25-30 incentive. A panel of 20-40 licensed plumbers and inspectors in the state visit and capture the three-photo protocol plus scratch and magnet test. Each point goes through AI classification, human QA, and tamper-evident geo-verification. Deliverables: (1) an evidence pack in the state inventory format; (2) an error-rate report with confidence intervals, including a non-response follow-up on a subset to measure bias; (3) a signed attestation the consultant can attach to the inventory submission. Where the state requires water-system oversight, the utility designates panel members as its agents in writing or witnesses by video. The sampling math is what makes it small: if 60 randomly sampled 'non-lead' lines are all non-lead, the true lead rate in that bin is below 5% with 95% confidence, and 150 clean lines bounds it below 2%.
why_now: First-round inventories leaned heavily on models, and reviewers, litigants and journalists are now questioning the unknown and 'non-lead' bins. The next inventory update cycle (around late 2027 under the federal rule, verify) is when models get challenged. Consultants are under fixed-fee pressure and want to avoid running field crews. Vision models plus tamper-evident capture make a small distributed audit panel cheaper than centrally staffed crews. Predictive modeling has reached the point where the constraint is credibility, not accuracy.
revenue_model: Wholesale price of about $140 per ground-truth point, against a cost of roughly $85-95 (panel payout $70-85, homeowner incentive, QA). An audit of one bin (60-150 points) is $9-21k, and a mid-size utility with three bins is a $30-40k engagement that fits under many small-purchase limits. Sold through the consultant as a pass-through with markup, or directly to the utility when the state reviewer requests it. Recurring revenue comes from an annual drift attestation ($10-15k per utility) as inventories are updated. A later product is a labeled, consented evidence dataset licensed back to modelers to retrain.
non_obvious_insight: A buyer that needs a sample, not a census, changes everything the judges worried about. Sixty to a few hundred points per utility means a 10-25% response rate is fine, thin opportunistic supply is fine, and per-point price can be $140 instead of $40. Every clean point vouches for thousands of predicted lines, so a sample point is worth far more to the buyer than a census point. The valuable thing to sell is independence: the model vendor cannot audit its own model, and the consulting firm that sells hourly field crews has no reason to keep the audit small.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 10 regional consulting firms and 3 state drinking-water programs. Ask what evidence the state wants to accept a modeled non-lead bin, and whether a third-party photo sample with utility authorization counts. Pick one state and one consultant with at least three active inventory contracts. Days 10-25: recruit 20 licensed inspectors and plumbers through local chapters and pay a launch rate. Draw a random sample of 60 from one predicted non-lead bin the consultant has already produced. Mail notices with the incentive and contact until 60 are visited. Days 25-30: deliver the evidence pack and a one-page error-rate memo at cost or free, and submit it to the state reviewer through the consultant. Ask for a paid audit of the next utility's three bins.
lineage: mutation of I0463 ('Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: BlueConduit, VODA.ai (Lead Finder / Lead Zero / Lead Management Dashboard), Trinnex leadCAST (used by Durham, NC), Esri ArcGIS Lead Service Line Inventory solution. White space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply. | How this version avoids them: It sells to BlueConduit, VODA.ai and Stantec-type firms as an input rather than competing with them, and it is neutral where BlueConduit's own field partners or a consultant's own crews are not, which makes it a credibility layer. Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123 and DIY self-ID forms collect voluntary owner submissions to fill the inventory, but none draws a random audit sample or produces a signed error-rate attestation. Electro Scan and Echologics hardware and RCAP door-to-door programs are verification methods that could be used as sample-collection tools, and a state may accept them, so they are potential partners rather than substitutes. A consultant or modeler that tries to build this in-house loses the independence that is the product. The parent's municipal sales cycle is replaced by consultants who already hold contract vehicles and small-purchase task orders.

title: Solos Refer, We File: National Delay-Suit Bench
one_liner: Invert the tool model: a lawyer-owned litigation bench that takes stuck cases referred by immigration solos, files at industrial speed for about 60% of the boutique price, and pays the referring lawyer a fee share, building a national referral network and the full-cycle dataset as a by-product.
customer: Payer: stuck applicants (post-interview N-400, I-751, I-765, long-idle I-130/I-140) referred by their own immigration lawyer, paying a $2,995 flat fee plus about $455 in costs. Channel: 1-10 attorney immigration firms in NY, NJ and CT that hold stuck clients but will not be counsel of record on a federal suit. Expansion: solos in any state, then boutique firms as overflow customers.
problem: The parent's model needs solos to pay $400 to do something they fear, and the research found no evidence that solos pay for tooling. What solos do have is client trust and a pile of stuck files. Their current choices are to do nothing or to refer the client to a boutique for no reward and the risk of losing the client. Meanwhile the one visible provider (Mandamus.com) is a small boutique with about 30 litigated petitions in 15 years, prices at $5,000 plus $500, and runs no co-counsel program for other lawyers. That leaves a large pool of unserved clients who cannot pay $5,000.
solution: A lawyer-owned litigation bench with the software company as management-services provider under a flat per-case fee (not a percentage of legal fees). The referral flow: a solo submits a stuck case through a 4-minute referral link or a case-management export; the ledger triages it (declining nationality-hold suits and Fifth Circuit I-485 claims); the client e-signs a fee-division consent that names each lawyer's share and the joint responsibility; the bench files within 72 hours, runs the 60-day clock, negotiates consent-order-first, and files the EAJA petition when a consent order supports it. The referring lawyer stays counsel on the underlying application, receives status in their own system, and earns 30% ($900) of the fee. The flat fee covers all litigation including an MTD opposition, matching the boutique's promise. Key legal gate: joint-responsibility fee division rules vary by state (NY 1.5(g) and ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) style), so launch only where ethics counsel clears it.
why_now: AI drafting and docket automation cut attorney time per routine filing from 6-10 hours to about 3 with paralegal support, which lets price fall to roughly 60% of the boutique at a healthy margin. The USAO's 45-90 day resolution pattern means one litigator can carry 60-100 live files, so the constraint on a litigation shop is intake, not lawyer time. Solos are overloaded and fear being first to file. The research found no co-counsel or referral program for other lawyers, so the economics of referral are unexploited.
revenue_model: Client pays $2,995 flat (court costs about $455 passed through). Referral share $900. Illustrative unit economics (assumptions): about $300 paralegal and attorney time, $40 service, about $225 expected tail (15% of cases x roughly $1,500 of MTD opposition work), $60 support, leaving about $1,450 contribution per case. 3,000 cases a year (a year-3 target that requires expanding the market, since the RECAP sample shows only 350-480 filings a year) would produce about $4.3M contribution. Upside: license the ledger, sell overflow capacity to boutiques, and reuse the same referral rails for other agency-delay claims (consular administrative processing, FOIA, passports).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not tooling but willingness to be counsel of record. Solos already own client trust and stuck files but earn nothing from referring out and fear the suit; a fee share for zero litigation risk turns them from prospects who must be persuaded to pay into an eager, unpaid-acquisition channel, at 30% of fee versus the boutique's SEO and ad spend. Because most cases moot in weeks, the bench recycles capacity fast, and it is the bench, not a tool, that naturally accumulates the full-cycle data (service date, USCIS action date, fee outcome) that makes the ledger better than anyone's public docket analytics. Scale economies and a referral network are both reachable within 24 months.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: get an ethics-counsel memo for NY, NJ and CT on joint-responsibility fee division and a flat-fee MSO; secure a lawyer cofounder or contract litigator admitted in E.D.N.Y., S.D.N.Y., D.N.J. and D. Conn. (the Mandamus.com boutique, admitted in D. Conn., D.D.C. and S.D. Tex., is a possible bench partner rather than only a rival); draft the referral agreement and client consent. Days 10-30: recruit 15 NY/NJ/CT solos through AILA chapters and direct outreach to attorneys of record on RECAP naturalization suits, pre-load 30 stuck cases from their own books, file the first 10 within 72 hours of consent, log every outcome, and pay the first referral share when the client pays. Go/no-go: 10 cases filed, more than half of referrers sending a second case, and modeled contribution of at least $1,000 per case.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com is a capacity-limited boutique acquiring clients by SEO at $5,000 and shows no co-counsel program; this acquires clients through lawyers who already hold them, prices at about 60% of the boutique, and can even contract the boutique's attorney as bench capacity. Docketwise has no litigation feature and is the natural place for a 'refer this case' button, so it is a channel, not a rival. Alma and Boundless have stuck clients and no litigation offer, so they are referral sources. Lex Machina, Trellis and CourtListener sell analytics or raw data, not filing capacity. DoNotPay and free pro se guides push risk onto the applicant; this puts a signed federal litigator behind every filing. Selective intake (no nationality-hold or Fifth Circuit I-485 cases) protects the win rate that competitors' broad templates cannot.

title: Load-Proven Warranty Wrap for Data Halls
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of chasing OEMs for owners as warranties expire, run a standardized load-proof test before expiry, fix what the OEM owes for free, then sell a capacity-backed warranty wrap that covers the post-expiry tail, priced from a proprietary fleet failure database.
customer: First buyers: owners and lenders' technical advisors of energized data halls approaching OEM warranty expiry, asking for a standardized Load-Proven test and certificate (a covenant-friendly document for refinancing or ABS). Later buyers: the same owners buying multi-year coverage for gensets, UPS, chillers and liquid-cooling CDUs. The capacity provider (a specialty insurer or reinsurer) is a third party in the money flow.
problem: The parent's contingency model is hard to collect and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds. Behind that is a bigger issue: once OEM warranties lapse, owners of AI halls with dense power and liquid cooling carry an unpriced failure tail, and nobody has independent load-tested failure data on these systems. OEM service contracts cover a single vendor's gear and are priced generically. Lenders financing GPU-era assets see equipment residual risk with no standard way to test or rate it.
solution: Phase 1, within 6 months: sell a standardized Load-Proven protocol. It is a 3-5 day staged load test (gensets, UPS and battery, chillers and CDUs, breakers), thermography, oil, coolant and battery diagnostics, using a load-bank rental partner and NETA-type testing subcontractors. Each test outputs a certificate and, where a defect shows, an OEM claim package while the OEM is still liable. Every test feeds a proprietary failure and degradation database. Phase 2, months 6-18: place multi-year tail coverage for tested gear through a broker or MGA partner on a quota-share basis with an insurer or reinsurer. Only gear that passed the test is bound. Defects surfaced by the test are repaired at the OEM's cost first, so the wrap covers a cleaner tail. Phase 3: become the MGA, and push the test protocol into loan covenants and insurer schedules as the standard.
why_now: AI halls introduce liquid-cooling and high-density power gear with immature public failure data, so generic pricing is either too expensive or blind. Data center lending and ABS need equipment-condition standards. Phase slippage means a large group of halls will pass through OEM expiry without ever having been stressed. Cheap LLM extraction of test logs and maintenance records lets a small team standardize reports across sites.
revenue_model: Phase 1: $60-120K per hall for the Load-Proven test (much of it load-bank pass-through), plus any claim-based fee. Phase 2: broker commission, then MGA ceding and profit commission on premium. Assumed pricing to validate with capacity providers: coverage at 1-2% of covered equipment value per year, and a 50 MW hall carries roughly $50-80M of gensets, UPS, chillers and switchgear, so about $0.5-1.6M of annual premium per hall and roughly $100-300K of commission to the MGA. That is on the order of 5-10x the parent's audit fee per hall.
non_obvious_insight: The inspection is both the revenue product and the underwriting filter, and the two feed each other. Defects found pre-expiry are paid by the OEM, which reduces adverse selection, and the resulting data is a cornered resource: independent, fleet-level, load-based, across OEMs. The parent treated the warranty as an asset to recover. The bigger business treats post-warranty risk as an asset class to price, using the only thing OEMs cannot easily replicate, which is neutral cross-vendor test data.
first_30_days: Draft a two-page Load-Proven protocol with a load-bank rental partner and a NETA-type test firm. Get one data-center-finance law firm or lender's technical advisor to review a one-page covenant template. Pitch three owners with halls approaching OEM expiry and one lender with a delayed-lease loan. Meet two equipment-breakdown or specialty warranty MGAs and ask what data they would need to quote a quota-share on tested MEP gear. Goal: one paid pilot test signed and one written indication of appetite from a capacity provider.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco, Anyset, Nomic, Equipment Warranty Log and CxPlanner document, track or review; none tests under load or takes risk. Wind EOW vendors, Sinovoltaics and TWAICE are asset-class specific and stop at the claim or the analytics. OEM riders and service contracts (Trane, Cummins, Eaton) are single-vendor and priced without neutral test data, which is the wedge for an independent wrap. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are hardware suppliers and channel partners. Because revenue moves from contingency-on-avoided-cost to premium, the collection and measurement flaws the judges named disappear. Defensibility comes from the failure database (cornered resource), covenant adoption (standard-setting) and later scale in premium volume.

title: Materials-Leakage Diligence for Trade-Shop Acquirers
one_liner: Sell search-fund, independent-sponsor and roll-up buyers of plumbing/HVAC shops a five-day report that reconciles the target's supplier spend to its customer invoices, sizes the fixable leak as EBITDA, and sets the baseline for a post-close capture program.
customer: Search-fund CEOs, independent sponsors and PE platform add-on teams buying residential plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops with $2-15M revenue, plus the SBA and ETA lenders and small quality-of-earnings shops that can white-label it. They are repeat or well-networked buyers who already spend on diligence and want a differentiated, quantified edge.
problem: Lower-middle-market trade deals are underwritten from a QuickBooks P&L and a seller-prepared add-back schedule. Gross margin looks acceptable or off, but the buyer cannot tell whether materials margin is real, leaking through unbilled truck-stock parts, or dragged by supplier price drift and stale pricebooks. Buyers discover the leak after closing, when the owner-operator's habits are theirs to fix. The parent idea has the same structural flaws sold to shop owners: owners feel a $10K fee is expensive and resist behavior change, and recoveries are hard to attribute. Generic accounting-firm quality-of-earnings work is done at general-ledger level, as far as I can tell, and rarely reconciles supplier spend to customer invoice lines, especially for shops this small.
solution: A fixed-scope, five-business-day 'Materials Truth Report' run in confirmatory diligence. The seller shares read-only QuickBooks and a field-service invoice export through the data room. The report gives (1) 24 months of Materials Capture Ratio (materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased) by job type, tech and supplier, compared with a pooled peer range; (2) supplier price position, meaning multiplier drift, surcharges and unclaimed credits versus the shop's own history; (3) truck-stock and inventory reasonableness; (4) a normalized gross-margin range for EBITDA underwriting; and (5) a 100-day capture plan with dollar values by lever (kit-based pricebook fixes, tech coaching, repricing file, supplier renegotiation). After closing, the buyer keeps the shop on a capture program measured against the diligence baseline, which was agreed pre-close and so cannot be disputed. Roll-ups get a portfolio dashboard comparing all acquired shops.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings since 2025 made materials margin the least trustworthy line in a trade shop's books, and buyers have been burned. HVAC and plumbing are consistently among the most-targeted sectors for search funds, independent sponsors and PE add-ons, so diligence differentiation is now a buyer priority. LLM parsing of supplier lines lets a two-person team deliver in a week what would otherwise be weeks of associate time. Field-service and accounting platforms expose exports, so a seller can share data in minutes.
revenue_model: Buyer pays $7,500 per target ($2,500 at engagement, $5,000 at close, or the full fee if delivered with the deal dead, negotiable). Post-close, either 20% of measured uplift over the diligence baseline for 12 months, or $500 per shop per month for roll-up portfolio monitoring. White-label to QoE boutiques and lenders at $3,000 wholesale per report. Value logic for the buyer: on a $6M shop, one point of revenue is $60K of EBITDA, worth roughly $200-350K of purchase price at 3.5-6x, so a $7.5K report is a rounding error next to the price adjustment or the 100-day plan value it produces.
non_obvious_insight: Changing the payer fixes three flaws at once. Authority: a new owner can change technician compensation, pricebook and process on day one, while an incumbent owner-operator rarely will. Attribution: the diligence baseline is a pre-agreed, third-party measurement, so uplift fees are not disputable. Willingness to pay: to a buyer the leak is enterprise value, not annual cash, so it justifies fees that would scare a shop owner. It also reverses the sales problem. Instead of selling to thousands of busy owners, you sell repeatedly to a few hundred networked buyers who talk to each other in search-fund and independent-sponsor communities, and each diligence adds a shop to the pooled benchmark without a per-shop sales effort. Roll-ups are the natural repeat customer and the natural distribution channel for the capture program.
first_30_days: Build a list of 40 search-fund and independent-sponsor buyers with live trade-shop deals (newsletters, ETA communities, LinkedIn, broker teasers). Offer the report free on one live deal in return for permission to cite anonymized findings. Aim for 3 live deals by day 30, with delivery within 5 business days of data access. In parallel, talk to two small QoE shops about white-labeling. Convert the first paid engagement on the next deal at $7,500. Position it as confirmatory diligence after an LOI, since sellers resist sharing invoice lines pre-LOI. Track whether the median target shows a capture gap worth more than $100K of EBITDA-equivalent, which tells you if buyers will keep paying. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so first check for any existing tech-enabled trade diligence vendors.
lineage: mutation of I0068 ('Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. What remains unserved is the customer-side leak: parts on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or pulled from truck stock, that never reached the customer invoice, plus supplier price drift and quoted-price violations tied back to the shop's own pricebook and markup targets. Existing tools (ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps, Ramp) are software the shop must adopt and operate, and they focus on paying suppliers correctly. Three parts are open: (1) shops on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge or Simpro, or ServiceTitan shops not using Procurement/AP, who have no PO-to-job workflow; (2) the done-for-you, no-recovery-no-fee commercial model, which no software vendor offers; (3) a cross-shop SKU price benchmark from pooled supply-house invoices. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces. | How this version avoids them: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps and Ramp all sell operating software to the shop, which must adopt it, keep POs and receipts clean, and run it weekly. This is a one-time attested analysis sold to the buyer, produced from an export of whatever field-service system and QuickBooks the target already uses, so nothing has to be adopted and it works on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge and ServiceTitan targets alike. ServiceTitan's statement and credit tools overlap only on the supplier-side piece, which here is a secondary section, not the product. No platform vendor has any incentive to produce third-party diligence on a shop being sold to a competitor, and MarginEdge-style tools are restaurant-only. The buyer relationship also gives a natural route into the parent's capture program after close without selling to the shop from scratch.

title: Site-Control Check for Utility Large-Load Queues
one_liner: A neutral 48-hour report on whether each large-load applicant really controls the land it names, sold to the utilities that must now screen speculative data center requests and billed through to the applicants.
customer: Large-load and interconnection managers, plus regulatory counsel, at G&T electric co-ops, municipal utilities and mid-size wires companies. Wedge: Texas co-ops, munis and mid-size TDUs (about 150 entities), then SPP and MISO states. The buyer is the utility. The applicant pays through the study-fee schedule.
problem: Utilities are buried in large-load requests, and many are speculative. The same parcel is shopped to several utilities. 'Site control' is often an applicant-supplied PDF or a non-binding LOI. The utility has to decide which requests get $100k+ studies and reserved capacity. A wrong guess strands capital or pushes cost onto ratepayers. Regulators and commissions now expect screening, but staff have no independent way to check control of land beyond what the applicant says.
solution:
The utility requires the applicant to list its parcels, and we do the rest.
1. Pull recorded instruments on those parcels and their neighbors from county portals, targeted per parcel with a landman fallback, so no bulk licence is needed.
2. Classify by reading the image rather than the clerk's label, and resolve the LLC family by notary, return-to firm and address.
3. Deliver a one-page Site-Control Report graded Recorded, Partial, Unrecorded or Conflicting. It shows acreage under recorded control against the acreage the claimed MW implies, option expiry dates, competing claimants, and duplicate-request flags across utilities through an opt-in hashed-parcel index.
4. Upsell a monthly territory sweep, which is the original Courthouse Tape, for assemblies that have not filed a request yet.
A human landman reviews every Partial or Conflicting result.
why_now: Utilities are being pushed to prove large-load requests are real. Texas SB 6 (2025) reportedly requires 75 MW+ applicants to show site control, disclose duplicate requests and pay study fees. Other utilities have added financial-commitment tariffs. ERCOT's large-load queue is reported at well over 200 GW, far beyond any buildable amount. LLM vision now reads messy recorded instruments accurately. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. Verify the SB 6 details before quoting them to customers.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per Site-Control Report, added as a pass-through line to the applicant's study-fee schedule. $60k-$150k a year per utility for the territory sweep, unlimited reports and a regulator-ready audit pack. Bottom-up: 60 utilities at about $80k is $4.8M ARR in Texas and neighboring states. 500 utilities nationally is about $40M ARR. Later add-on: applicants buy a neutral verified-site-control certificate to speed their queue position.
non_obvious_insight: Verification is much easier than detection. Because the utility can compel the parcel list, we skip the hardest parts of the parent: not knowing where to look, statewide bulk scraping, and false positives. A missing or unrecorded instrument becomes a finding in its own right, which also dodges the doubt that developers may not record option memos before announcement. Only a utility-side neutral can build the moat. Developers shop the same parcel to many utilities, and no utility will share its queue with a vendor that also sells to developers. A cross-utility duplicate-parcel index is therefore a network effect that Enverus or Paces cannot build without losing the trust of their own developer customers.
first_30_days: Take Texas. Call 25 co-op and muni large-load contacts through the Texas Electric Cooperatives and Texas Public Power Association networks and the NRECA circuit. Offer a free retrospective audit of each utility's last 10 requests using only recorded instruments. Report what share had no recorded control, duplicate claims or expired options. Convert two utilities to $20k-$30k paid pilots on new requests. In parallel, confirm which county portals allow per-parcel commercial retrieval and line up two landmen for offline counties.
lineage: mutation of I0773 ('Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. | How this version avoids them: Every competitor in the research sells to developers or investors. Enverus, Paces, GridCARE and DC Byte help a developer find or defend its own site, so utilities cannot treat them as neutral verifiers of a developer's claim. Cleanview and Heatmap Pro start at permit or news, which is after the queue decision. ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds and LLC piercing but not options, leases or easements, and do no per-request verification. Pandell manages a client's own documents. We sell only to the utility side, never to developers, and the audit trail suits a regulator. The remaining risk is Enverus adding the feature, so the cross-utility index and utility trust are the defence.

title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.

Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.

title: Materials Capture Ratio: Pay-on-Lift for Flat-Rate Shops
one_liner: Measure what share of the parts a residential plumbing or HVAC shop buys actually reaches a customer invoice, coach the leak out tech by tech and job type, and charge 25% of the measured lift over a frozen baseline.
customer: Owner and office manager of residential plumbing and HVAC service-and-replacement shops with 8-25 trucks and $2-8M revenue. They run flat-rate pricing on Housecall Pro, FieldEdge or Jobber (or ServiceTitan without Procurement/AP) plus QuickBooks Online, and techs pull from truck stock restocked on account at Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local house. First job types are water heater replacement and condenser/air-handler swaps, where the standard install kit is well defined (expansion tank, flex connectors, T&P valve, discharge pipe, gas flex, line set, disconnect, pad, whip). Reached through PHCC chapters and owner masterminds.
problem: The parent idea has three weak spots. (1) Retroactive found money is mostly uncollectible. A homeowner will not pay a $40 parts add-on six months after a completed job, so an audit that reports history overpromises. Real value is capturing correctly from now on. (2) Contingency on 'newly captured revenue' cannot be attributed, so owners will dispute the fee. (3) Ticket-to-job matching from emailed PDFs is messy because counter tickets carry a typed job name at best, and these shops have no PO-per-job discipline for a 3-way match. Meanwhile the recurring leak is real and habitual. Techs bill labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring or the whip, and nobody sees it because the two ledgers (supply-house spend and customer invoices) are never divided into each other.
solution: Lead with one owner-legible KPI, the Materials Capture Ratio (MCR): materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased at cost, by month, tech, job type and supplier. It is computed from two exports and needs no invoice-by-invoice matching. Read-only OAuth into QuickBooks Online pulls supply-house bills and restock POs. A CSV or API export from the field-service software supplies the invoice material lines. Day one output is 'of every $100 of parts you buy, you bill $X', per tech. Then learn the shop's own kit per top-10 flat-rate job type by parsing a sample of supply-house lines with an LLM, and each week send the office manager a missing-parts list: closed jobs whose invoice lacks items the kit says were bought, with the pricebook item ready to add, plus which are still rebillable (open T&M, commercial, home-warranty and maintenance-agreement jobs). Add a pre-invoice nudge in the tech's flow later. Supplier-side price drift, unclaimed return credits and repricing files are a free add-on from the same data, not the headline. Contract: freeze a 6-month baseline MCR from the export, then charge 25% of (MCR lift x purchases x the shop's own average materials markup) for 12 months, with the shop's accountant signing the baseline once. It converts to a $199-499 per month subscription that includes the peer MCR benchmark.
why_now: Tariff-driven list-price moves mean flat-rate pricebooks go stale in a quarter, so owners are already asking where margin went. LLMs make it cheap to learn a shop's per-job kit from messy supplier lines. QuickBooks Online and the field-service platforms now expose APIs and exports, so onboarding takes minutes rather than a consulting project. The 2025 copper, steel and aluminum tariff regime, per the parent's research, made materials cost the most volatile line in a service shop's P&L.
revenue_model: Year one is a pay-on-lift fee of 25% of measured incremental materials revenue over the frozen baseline (no lift, no fee), which pairs a low-risk sale with a clean way to dispute-proof attribution. Then a $199-499 per month monitoring and benchmark subscription. Illustration: a $4M shop that lifts capture by 1-2% of revenue recovers $40-80K a year and we earn $10-20K in year one. If the median shop's gap is under 0.5% of revenue, the hypothesis is falsified within 30 days.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the found dollars. It is the rate of capture, a ratio you can compute from two exports without matching one ticket to one job, which sidesteps the parsing problem and the retroactive-billing problem together. Pegging the fee to a pre-agreed baseline ratio makes the contingency indisputable, which the parent lacked. Level is not the point, since warranty parts, callbacks and inventory build legitimately lower MCR. What matters is the delta and the spread between techs on the same job type, and that spread turns a vague back-office audit into a coaching scoreboard the owner can act on Monday morning. Pooled over many shops, the per-job-type kit and the MCR distribution become the cornered data asset.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 8 shops from PHCC chapters and owner masterminds on Housecall Pro, Jobber or FieldEdge with QuickBooks Online. Get read-only QBO access and one invoice-line export each. Days 7-10: compute MCR by tech and by job type in a notebook and deliver a one-page 'you buy $100, bill $X' result within 48 hours of data. Days 10-20: learn the water-heater and condenser-swap kits from supply-house lines, and produce the missing-parts list for the last 60 days as a coaching artifact, not a bill. Day 14-30: ask each shop to sign a 12-month pay-on-lift agreement with the baseline frozen from the export, and start the weekly missing-parts email. Kill test: if the median gap between the top-quartile and bottom-quartile tech MCR is under 3 points, or shops will not accept the baseline, drop or pivot. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so also manually check r/HVAC, r/Plumbing and Crunchbase for small funded entrants before spending on building.
lineage: mutation of I0068 ('Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ServiceTitan Accounts Payable (bill inbox, 3-way matching, Manage Statements, Manage Credits, discrepancy flags), Kojo, BuildOps (Procurement and Payables), Fergus. White space: Nobody I found offers a contingency-fee, done-for-you recovery audit for trade shops. I found no evidence anyone has assembled that for residential and light-commercial trade shops. ServiceTitan's Manage Statements and Manage Credits are the closest overlap with the returns-credit and price-error pieces. | How this version avoids them: It drops the supplier-invoice-audit-software pitch that collides with ServiceTitan AP, Kojo and BuildOps, all of which police what the shop pays suppliers via PO and receipt 3-way matching. It sells the customer-side billing leak they do not market, and it works without POs, receipts or job-level ticket matching, so it fits Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops and ServiceTitan shops that never turned on Procurement/AP, the segment the parent's research called uncontested. Kojo and BuildOps are built for larger commercial contractors with PO discipline, Ramp is a horizontal AP tool, and MarginEdge serves restaurants. No one offers an outcome-priced, done-for-you service, and the supplier-side price-drift findings are a bundled extra rather than a head-on feature fight. Platform risk is limited because a field-service vendor that earns on payments and pricebooks has little reason to audit an owner's tech-by-tech compliance and publish peer benchmarks.

title: Placement Proof for Workforce Pell Providers
one_liner: A verified job-placement and completion ledger that makes short-term training programs (CDL, CNA, welding, HVAC, medical assistant, cosmetology) audit-ready for the governor and Secretary approvals that Workforce Pell requires.
customer: Small proprietary career schools, community college workforce and continuing-education units, and employer-training nonprofits running 8-15 week programs. The program owner or director pays. State workforce boards are a second buyer because they were given no new resources to verify placement.
problem: The Workforce Pell final rule (published May 19, 2026; effective July 20, 2026, with early implementation from July 1) covers programs of 150-599 clock hours and 8-15 weeks. A program must show 70% completion and 70% job placement, measured over the 12 months before it applies and annually after that. The governor must first certify the program as high-skill, high-wage or in-demand, then the Secretary approves. Providers must submit completer lists and the information needed to verify placement. Commenters flagged burden for small providers and noted states got no new resources to run the framework. Separately, the earnings-premium rule (effective July 1, 2027) strips Direct Loan access from programs that fail in two of three consecutive years. The Department estimated 93% of cosmetology programs would fail under the proposal.
solution: At completion the system automatically sends completers and employers text and email verification requests at 30, 90 and 180 days. It collects pay stubs, employer confirmations and consent for state wage-record matching, and reconciles them to the rule's placement definition. It produces the governor's application packet (completer list, placement evidence, tuition versus earnings benchmarks) and the annual recertification. It also scores each existing program's exposure to the earnings-premium test using public program-level earnings data so owners can decide what to keep, fix or convert into a short-term program.
why_now: The 12-month look-back means a provider that is not tracking verified placement now cannot apply in 2027. The earnings-premium test takes effect July 1, 2027 and is already being scored on 2021 completers' 2025 earnings. States are building governor-approval processes this fall, and Workforce Pell went live July 2026.
revenue_model: $4-12k per year per program subscription, or $150-300 per completer verified. $3-5k fixed fee for the governor application packet. Earnings-premium exposure report for $1.5-3k. Later, licensing to state workforce boards for verification.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint is not program design but evidence: 70% verified placement with a 12-month clock that starts before the application. Short-course providers such as CDL, CNA and barbering schools typically track completion, not verified employment, so most will discover the gap after the clock has started. The final rule requires providers to give the Governor 'necessary information to verify the job placement rate', and it aggregates small programs' completers up to four award years to reach a 30-student minimum, which favors providers with clean historical records. The Title IV survival angle (93% of cosmetology programs were projected to fail the earnings test under the proposal) gives the same customer a second, more urgent reason to buy. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/19/2026-10013/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand-driven-workforce-pell-pell-grant and https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/01/2026-13286/accountability-in-higher-education-and-access-through-demand--driven-workforce-pell-student-tuition
first_30_days: Pick two states whose governors have opened a Workforce Pell approval process. Recruit five schools in different fields, including one at-risk cosmetology school, with a $1.5k pilot price. Backfill the last 12 months of completers by text and employer email to produce a baseline verified placement rate. Deliver a sample governor packet and an earnings-premium exposure score for each. Use the results to pitch the state workforce board on verification capacity.

Structural risks visible without further research: (a) if the final rule lets states verify placement from UI wage records, a self-collected pay-stub product loses much of its value; (b) SIS vendors can bolt this on as a feature; (c) the number of approved programs, and so the buyer count, may be small at first.

title: One Binder Scan: Lender Monitoring Plus Warranty Recovery
one_liner: One AI read of a data hall's closeout binders yields both a lender's ready-for-service probability and an owner's serial-level warranty ledger, with contingency warranty recovery as the reason the owner grants access.
customer: Private credit funds, banks and insurers lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts (pay a fixed monitoring fee). Colo developers, powered-shell landlords and neocloud owners with energized but idle halls (pay a share of recovered warranty value).
problem: Lenders need interior truth about the last 90 days before ready-for-service but borrowers resist giving data-room access to a monitor. Owners of energized-but-empty halls don't know their OEM warranty clocks are silently running out. Both parties need the same documents (gear serials, startup sheets, Cx reports, integrated test results, punch lists) and neither has staff to read them.
solution: An LLM pipeline ingests POs, bills of lading, startup sheets, Cx sign-offs and maintenance logs into one serial-level ledger. Lender view: a Readiness Ladder score with probability of ready-for-service by date, covenant and draw triggers, and OEM startup-tech calendar risk. Owner view: warranty expiry dates, voiding conditions, and a hit list of claims and start-date deferrals to file within 90-120 days. Sold as a $25K two-week lender second opinion, made economical by a contingency warranty scan (25-30% of recoveries) offered free to the owner. Structure the two views as separate teams with an information wall, and route recoveries through the lender-controlled operating account so the independence of the monitor is not compromised.
why_now: About half of 2026 US capacity is slipping and neocloud credit is a live worry, so lenders are capping exposure. Many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak, tariff-inflated prices, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. Satellites have commoditized the exterior, leaving the interior (binders and commissioning data) as the scarce truth. LLMs now read messy closeout binders cheaply.
revenue_model: Lender side: $25K two-week second opinions, $40-120K full pre-close diligence, $8-20K per month per facility monitoring. Owner side: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and deferrals, $150-400 per asset per year tracking, $15-40K closeout audits, and PO-stage clause packs that defer warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty ledger and the readiness score are built from the same binder, so the second product costs almost nothing to produce. The biggest barrier to interior monitoring is borrower cooperation, and a free contingency service that recovers money is the best incentive to provide it. Expiring warranties and unavailable OEM startup techs are also leading indicators of delay, so each product improves the other's signal. The lender's covenant becomes the distribution channel to owners at the moment they have binders and idle halls. Ethyco offers warranty-phase support but not idle-hall contingency or lender integration.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Find 3 owner-operators through Cx and PM networks whose halls energized 8-11 months ago and are not fully loaded, and offer a free 10-day binder scan on contingency. Build the extraction on real binders (gensets, UPS and chillers first) and deliver an 'expiring in 90 days' hit list. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and pitch 5-10 private credit desks a $25K two-week second opinion on one live deal, using the scan as proof of depth.
lineage: hybrid of I0365 + I0229 (Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders + Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls). Why stronger: Double revenue from one document-processing pipeline, with two payers whose interests line up. Owners get paid to be monitored, lenders get better collateral and cleaner data, and access friction disappears. A serial-number equipment register across financed halls becomes a data moat that single-purpose competitors (satellite monitors or Cx firms) cannot replicate.
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SynMax Vulcan (with Industrial Info Resources data partnership), Currence (formerly Sightline Climate), Epoch AI Frontier Data Centers Hub, SemiAnalysis (consulting, AI Datacenter Model, ClusterMAX). White space: The unserved wedge is narrow but real. (1) No product found in this session combines a binary, evidence-backed 'Readiness Ladder' for the last 90 days before RFS (utility energization letter, MV gear energization, Cx Level 4/5 and IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush and pressure tests, fiber acceptance, punch-list burn-down, OEM startup-tech availability) with a probabilistic RFS-by-date output and draw or covenant triggers. (2) Satellite and database vendors (SynMax, IIR, Currence, Epoch) cover the exterior and the announced schedule, and their materials do not claim commissioning or energization evidence. (3) GPU-deal technical advisors, as described by Peony, focus on fleet, telemetry and power documents rather than data hall commissioning. (4) Traditional IEs are slow, tied to a single lender or borrower, and priced for large project-finance deals. A fixed-fee, two-week, desk-plus-site 'second opinion' for a private credit desk, insurer or offtaker appears unserved. (5) The offtaker and backstop side (AI labs signing take-or-pay capacity, Google or Nvidia-style backstop providers) is structurally underserved because IEs work for lenders. Risks: incumbent IEs and Cx firms can add this as a service line, SemiAnalysis could bolt it on, and the business is people-bound (bench of ex-Cx leads) with limited software moat. Access to sites, contractors and Cx records depends on borrower cooperation, which means lender-imposed information covenants or offtaker leverage. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline.
